findings.title: Pre-existing local recovery-codes credential is left behind when codes are written to user storage
findings.body: `createRecoveryCodesCredential` delegates to `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)` and, as soon as some user storage provider accepts the codes (`userStorageCreated == true`), it returns without touching Keycloak's own credential store. If the user already has a `recovery-authn-codes` credential stored locally (codes configured before the federation provider supported the type, while the provider was disabled, or for a user whose provider capabilities changed), that stale credential is never removed. `SubjectCredentialManager.isValid` falls back to the local credential providers when the user-storage validator rejects an input, so the *old* codes keep authenticating the user indefinitely even after the user regenerated codes. The helper should delete existing local credentials of this type when the provider takes over (and vice versa), otherwise credential rotation can be bypassed.

findings.title: Undocumented and asymmetric value format passed to user storage providers for recovery codes
findings.body: The credential value handed to the user storage provider is a Jackson-serialized JSON array of the raw recovery codes (`JsonSerialization.writeValueAsString(generatedCodes)`), whereas validation of the very same credential type passes a *single* raw code (`UserCredentialModel.buildFromBackupAuthnCode(...)` in `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator`). This asymmetric wire format is not documented anywhere (no javadoc on the new method, no provider documentation in this PR). Any existing third-party `CredentialInputUpdater` that returns true from `supportsCredentialType("recovery-authn-codes")` - which today is only needed for validation - will now silently receive the JSON blob in `updateCredential` and will most likely store it as if it were a single code, corrupting the user's credential. The contract (JSON array of raw, unhashed codes on update; single raw code on validate) must be documented, or a dedicated structured input type used.

findings.title: User label and generation timestamp are dropped when the credential goes to user storage
findings.body: `createRecoveryCodesCredential` receives a fully built `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel` (containing the user label entered in the required-action form and the `generatedAt` timestamp validated against the auth-session note), but when delegating to user storage it only forwards the codes JSON in `new UserCredentialModel("", type, recoveryCodesJson)`. The provider therefore cannot store the label or creation date (the test provider in this PR invents `Time.currentTimeMillis()` and leaves the label null), so the label a user typed is silently lost and credential metadata shown in the account console differs from the local-storage behaviour.

findings.title: removeStoredCredentialById called with the id of a credential that may live in user storage
findings.body: After the lookup was changed to `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(...)`, the returned credential can originate from the user storage provider (`getFederatedCredentialsStream()`). Such a model is built by the provider and generally carries no Keycloak credential id (the test provider in this PR builds it via `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(...)`, which leaves `id == null`). Calling `authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(null)` on the exhausted-codes path either throws (JPA `find` with a null id raises `IllegalArgumentException`, producing a 500 during login) or is a no-op, and in no case does it clear the exhausted codes from the external store. The removal must be restricted to locally stored credentials (or delegated to the provider).

findings.title: Unguarded Optional.get() can now fail for credentials held in user storage
findings.body: `credentialModelOpt.get()` throws `NoSuchElementException` when no credential model is found. With this PR the codes may be stored in a user storage provider, and providers are not required to expose them: `CredentialInputUpdater.getCredentials` defaults to an empty stream, so a provider that stores and validates recovery codes but does not implement `getCredentials` makes `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential` return `Optional.empty()` while `isConfiguredFor` is still true. The authenticator then renders this login bean and the recovery-code login page fails with a 500 instead of asking for a code. The bean must handle the empty case (e.g. fall back to code number 0 / render without a specific index).

findings.title: Reference user-storage implementation never consumes a recovery code, and no test covers single use
findings.body: `isValid` for `recovery-authn-codes` only checks membership in the stored list and never invalidates the matched code; `getCredentials` additionally rebuilds the credential from the raw list each time, so every code is always reported as unused and the login form always requests code #0. Recovery codes are single-use by definition, so this provider (which is the de-facto reference implementation other provider authors will copy) accepts the same code an unlimited number of times. The new `testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` only logs in once and therefore does not verify that a used code is rejected, nor that the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action is re-triggered once all codes are consumed - exactly the behaviour that distinguishes recovery codes from a static secret.

findings.title: getCredentials dereferences a possibly null MyUser
findings.body: `var myUser = getMyUser(user);` is used without a null check at line 235 (`myUser.recoveryCodes`), while every other method in this class (`getDisableableCredentialTypesStream`, `isConfiguredFor`, `isValid`) explicitly guards against `getMyUser(user) == null`. If `getCredentials` is invoked for a user that is no longer in the in-memory map (e.g. after `removeUser`, or for a cached `UserModel`), the provider throws a NullPointerException instead of returning an empty stream, which will surface as a server error in whatever credential listing triggered the call.

findings.title: Credential returned by getCredentials loses its id and user label
findings.body: The `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel` built in `getCredentials` is created with `createFromValues(...)`, which does not carry over `myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()` (nor the stored label, which is always null because `updateCredential` never sets one). Consumers therefore get a credential with a null id: the browser authenticator passes exactly this id to `removeStoredCredentialById` on the exhausted-codes path, and account/admin REST cannot reference or delete the credential. The stored id should be set on the returned model.

findings.title: testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin never completes the login and ignores the logout result
findings.body: Unlike the sibling tests (`testOTPUpdateAndLogin`, `testLoginSuccess`), this test calls `testAppHelper.startLogin(...)` but never calls `testAppHelper.completeLogin()`, so the authorization code is never exchanged and the test only checks the redirect URL rather than that the login actually produced tokens. It then calls `testAppHelper.logout()` without asserting the result; since no id token/refresh token was obtained, the logout can silently fail, leaving the SSO cookie and user session alive for the following tests in this class (which reuse the same realm, browser and username `otp1`), making those tests order-dependent.
